#### `users`

Customer identity. Deliberately minimal under the Ghana Data Protection Act: phone number (required — it is the account key AND the payment instrument), one optional first name, no address, no ID document, no date of birth. Erasure is a soft delete plus a purge job that keeps only the aggregated money rows required by law. username defaults to phone_local so the Wi-Fi login is the number the customer already knows.

#### `wallet_entries`

Append-only credit ledger behind users.wallet_pesewas. This exists because in Ghana the practical remedy for a failed activation or a duplicate MoMo charge is often wallet credit, not a Paystack reversal — operator refunds can take days. Every balance change is one row here, so a dispute is answerable with a query. balance_after_pesewas makes gaps and double-applies visible.

#### `user_devices`

Registered devices per account. Two distinct controls live here: (1) the SIMULTANEOUS limit — enforced by FreeRADIUS via the Simultaneous-Use reply attribute derived from plans.max_simultaneous_devices; (2) the REGISTERED/bound limit — plans.max_registered_devices rows here, and when is_bound = true the edge FreeRADIUS policy rejects an Access-Request whose Calling-Station-Id is not in this table, which is what actually stops account sharing. A MAC seen once is auto-registered as pending until the customer or an admin allows it.

#### `sessions`

Server-side session store for BOTH the customer portal and the admin dashboard. Opaque random cookie value, only its sha256 stored, HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax. Customer sessions are short (2h sliding) because a shared family phone is the common case; admin sessions are 8h absolute and die on password or TOTP change. Storing them in the DB rather than a signed JWT gives us a "log out everywhere" button and revocation on ban — which matters when you suspend an account for abuse.

#### `phone_verifications`

OTP challenges. The code is hashed with a server-side pepper so a database leak does not hand over live OTPs. Rate limiting is enforced on THREE axes at once: per phone (cooldown_until, max 3 per 15 min), per IP (max 10 per hour), and per attempt count (5 tries then the challenge dies). OTP SMS costs money, so this table is also the defence against someone draining the Arkesel balance.

#### `rate_profiles`

Reusable bandwidth ceilings, rendered by the backend into the Mikrotik-Rate-Limit RADIUS reply attribute.   *** rx/tx ARE FROM THE ROUTER'S POINT OF VIEW — READ THIS TWICE ***   MikroTik documents Mikrotik-Rate-Limit as:     rx-rate[/tx-rate] [rx-burst-rate[/tx-burst-rate] [rx-burst-threshold[/tx-burst-threshold]                      [rx-burst-time[/tx-burst-time] [priority] [rx-rate-min[/tx-rate-min]]]]   where "rx is client UPLOAD and tx is client DOWNLOAD". So a plan sold as   "10 down / 5 up" must be rendered as  upload/download  =>  "5M/10M".   Getting this backwards is the most common MikroTik billing bug in existence and   it presents as "customers are slow" with no error anywhere.   Worked example, download_kbps=10000, upload_kbps=5000, burst 20000/10000 with   thresholds 10000/5000 for 12s, priority 8:     Mikrotik-Rate-Limit = "5M/10M 10M/20M 5M/10M 12s/12s 8"   Order in the string is: rate, burst-rate, burst-threshold, burst-time, priority.   burst-threshold is an average RATE in bits/s (not a byte allowance): burst is   permitted only while the average over burst-time stays below it. If thresholds   are omitted MikroTik uses rx-rate/tx-rate; if burst-time is omitted it uses 1s.   priority 1 = highest, 8 = lowest. rate-min may not exceed rate.   Burst is what makes a GH¢5 daily plan feel fast on a phone while still capping   the aggregate: the customer gets 20 Mbps for the first seconds of activity,   then settles to 10. Normalising this into its own table means several plans can   share a profile and a speed change is one UPDATE, not N.

#### `network_rules`

Block/allow list, edited in the dashboard and RENDERED to a RouterOS script (Phase 3 deliverable) rather than pushed live. enforcement says how it lands: dns = a DNS forwarder rule on the edge box (cheap, catches most, trivially bypassed by DoH — so also ship a DoH block); address_list = /ip firewall address-list + filter drop; layer7 = for URL prefixes that survive TLS only via SNI; walled_garden = the inverse, for the payment/SMS/portal domains that must stay reachable for an UNAUTHENTICATED client. category=bandwidth_hog is the honest one for a Starlink backhaul: blocking video CDNs on the cheap plans protects everyone else.

#### `subscriptions`

One row per purchased entitlement period — a ledger, not a mutable "current plan". Buying a second month while the first is still running creates a row with status=scheduled and starts_at = current.expires_at, which is what makes "renew early and keep your remaining days" work honestly. subscriptions_one_active_per_user (a PARTIAL unique index) guarantees at most one live entitlement per customer at the database level, so a webhook delivered twice cannot give someone two concurrent plans. The snapshot_* columns freeze price, cap, speed and device limits at the moment of purchase: an admin repricing a plan next month must not silently downgrade a customer who already paid.

#### `payment_attempts`

One row per try at collecting money. An order can have several: the customer fails on Telecel, retries on MTN, then pays by card. `reference` is OURS (WV-<orderRef>-<n>) and is what Paystack echoes back — it is the join key for webhooks and verify calls, and it is unique so a replayed webhook cannot attach to the wrong attempt.   The status machine mirrors what Paystack actually returns from POST /charge for Ghana MoMo:     pay_offline (MTN, AirtelTigo) -> approve the prompt on the phone -> charge.success webhook     send_otp    (Telecel)         -> customer dials *110#, we POST /charge/submit_otp     pending                       -> wait >=10s, then GET /transaction/check_pending/:reference   display_text is stored because it is the operator-specific instruction we must show verbatim ("Please dial *110#...") — inventing our own copy here is how customers get stuck.   CRITICAL: response envelope status:true does NOT mean the charge succeeded. Only data.status does. See docs/08-security.md.

#### `payment_events`

The webhook INBOX. Every inbound event is INSERTed here FIRST, in its own transaction, before any business logic runs — and the insert is the idempotency gate. `dedupe_key` is a unique index over a hash of (provider, event, data.id, data.status, data.reference), because Paystack does not supply an event UUID and WILL redeliver the same event whenever we answer anything other than 2xx. A duplicate therefore hits a unique violation and the handler returns 200 immediately without re-activating a subscription. body_hash catches a replayed body under a different event key. signature_valid records whether x-paystack-signature (HMAC-SHA512 of the RAW body with the secret key) verified — we still persist failed ones, because a signature failure is a security_event worth keeping evidence of.

#### `usage_records`

The cloud copy of RADIUS accounting, pushed by the edge node in batches. origin_id is a UNIQUE constraint, which is what makes the uplink idempotent: the edge keeps a local outbox and retries until the cloud acks, so a flaky Starlink link can never double-count a customer's data. user_id / subscription_id are resolved by username at ingest time so the dashboard never joins on a text username.   NOTE on octets: FreeRADIUS/MikroTik report 32-bit counters that WRAP at 4 GiB. The edge agent widens them using Acct-Input-Gigawords / Acct-Output-Gigawords and de-wraps across interim updates; if it cannot, it marks source=reconciled. Getting this wrong silently under-bills heavy users — see docs/04-freeradius.md.   Retention: raw rows kept 13 months, then folded into usage_daily and purged. Scale step at >20M rows: convert to monthly RANGE partitioning on acct_start_time (documented in docs/02-database-schema.md); BRIN indexing makes the unpartitioned version fine well past 10M.

#### `vouchers`

Individual prepaid codes. status transitions are enforced with a conditional UPDATE (where status = 'unused' and version = :v), not just app logic, so two people redeeming the same code at the same instant on two phones cannot both succeed. redeem_attempts is capped (5 per code, 20 per IP per hour) because voucher guessing is the number one attack on this kind of system; codes carry ~60 bits of Crockford-base32 entropy plus a check digit, and every miss is written to security_events as voucher_guessing. CSV/PDF export writes exported_at so a reprint is deliberate.

#### `messages`

Every SMS we send, with its delivery outcome. dedupe_key is the mechanism that stops a customer getting four "your plan expires in 2 days" messages when the reminder job retries — the job computes a deterministic key and the unique index does the rest.   DELIVERY REPORTS: Arkesel POSTs (query params sms_id + status) to the callback_url we pass, IN BATCHES, and the endpoint is UNAUTHENTICATED by design. So the handler must look sms_id up in provider_message_id and reject anything unknown; it must never trust a status for a message it did not send. That is the whole security model of the delivery callback and it is easy to get wrong.

#### `jobs`

A Postgres-backed work queue (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). Deliberately NOT Redis/BullMQ: one fewer service to run, one fewer thing to lose state in, and the queue is transactional with the business data it acts on — an order cannot be committed without its reminder job in the same transaction. Vercel Cron hits /internal/cron/tick every minute to drain it; a second worker is safe because SKIP LOCKED serialises claiming. Kinds: reminder.expiry_d2, reminder.expiry_d0, subscription.expire, subscription.grace_end, order.expire_abandoned, payment.poll_pending, usage.rollup, revenue.rollup, radius.reconcile, settlement.reconcile, sms.delivery_sync, retention.purge_login_attempts, retention.purge_usage, backup.verify.

## Edge node database (on-site) — RADIUS projection

Stock FreeRADIUS rlm_sql tables plus sync machinery. 15 tables. Never holds prices, payments or the authoritative subscription.

Source: `db/migrations/0002_edge_radius.sql` — 15 tables, 0 views, 0 functions, 19 indexes.

### Tables

#### `radacct`

Live RADIUS accounting, stock FreeRADIUS 3.0.x PostgreSQL layout. rlm_sql INSERTs on Accounting-Request Start, UPDATEs on Interim-Update and closes the row on Stop.   *** THE 4 GiB COUNTER WRAP ***   MikroTik reports Acct-Input-Octets / Acct-Output-Octets as 32-bit counters that   wrap at 4294967296, carrying the overflow in Acct-Input-Gigawords /   Acct-Output-Gigawords. A heavy user on a fast plan crosses 4 GiB in about   35 minutes at 20 Mbps, so on the GH¢100 plan this is a DAILY event, not an edge   case. Mishandled, the customer appears to use almost nothing and you silently   give away hundreds of gigabytes.   wavly_counter_suspect is set by syncd when the delta between two interim updates   is negative or implausibly large — i.e. a wrap it could not resolve. Those rows   are still uploaded (flagged) so the discrepancy is visible rather than hidden.   wavly_synced_at / wavly_origin_id are the uplink bookkeeping: a row is written to   sync_outbox in the same transaction it is closed, and origin_id becomes   usage_records.origin_id in the cloud, where a UNIQUE constraint makes retries   idempotent across a flaky Starlink link.   Open sessions (acctstoptime IS NULL) are the truth for "who is online now" and   for Simultaneous-Use enforcement.

#### `radgroupreply`

WHERE RATE LIMITING ACTUALLY LIVES. Groups are named after the RATE PROFILE,   not the plan — e.g. group "rate-12000-6000" carries       Mikrotik-Rate-Limit = "6M/12M 12M/24M 6M/12M 15s/15s 5"   Remember rx/tx are from the ROUTER'S point of view: rx = client UPLOAD,   tx = client DOWNLOAD. A plan sold as "12 down / 6 up" is written "6M/12M".   Getting this backwards is the most common MikroTik billing bug and it fails   silently, presenting only as "the internet is slow".   Also present: group "fup-rate-4000-2000" (fair-usage ceiling) and group   "suspended" carrying Auth-Type := Reject.   Because a plan's speed is group MEMBERSHIP rather than a per-user row, changing   the speed of 80 customers is one UPDATE here plus 80 CoA packets — not 80 row   edits, and not 80 chances to get one wrong.

Accepted and rejected authentications — the evidence trail for "it says my   password is wrong".   *** DATA PROTECTION — THIS OVERRIDE IS NOT OPTIONAL ***   The stock FreeRADIUS postauth query writes the SUBMITTED CLEARTEXT PASSWORD into   the `pass` column. Under the Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) that is   unnecessary processing of a secret, and a leaked edge database would hand over   every customer's Wi-Fi password. In mods-config/sql/main/postgresql/queries.conf   the post-auth query is overridden to write the literal string 'REDACTED'.   `pass` is nullable here so that override can also write NULL. Username, reply and   authdate are retained — that is everything a dispute actually needs.

#### `sync_outbox`

DURABLE UPLINK BUFFER — the write-ahead log that makes an eventually-consistent   design safe. Accounting is queued here in the SAME transaction it is written to   radacct, so a session recorded locally can never be lost before upload.   The agent drains it in batches of `radius.usage_push_batch_size` (200) to   POST /internal/edge/usage. The cloud dedupes on origin_id, which has a UNIQUE   constraint on usage_records — so a retry after a Starlink dropout mid-POST cannot   double-count a customer's data. Backoff is exponential with jitter, capped at   15 minutes, up to 200 attempts (~2 days of outage tolerance).   A three-day outage delays your dashboard. It never loses a billable byte.

| Column | Type | Null | Default / Generated | Keys & constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `bigserial` | no |  | **PK** |
| `origin_id` | `uuid` | no | gen_random_uuid() |  |
| `kind` | `text` | no |  | CHECK |
| `payload` | `jsonb` | no |  |  |
| `status` | `text` | no | 'pending' | CHECK |
| `attempts` | `integer` | no | 0 |  |
| `max_attempts` | `integer` | no | 200 |  |
| `next_retry_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |
| `last_error` | `text` | yes |  |  |
| `acked_at` | `timestamptz` | yes |  |  |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |

_Indexes:_
- `sync_outbox_pending_idx` — `status`, `next_retry_at` PARTIAL
- `sync_outbox_brin` — BRIN `created_at`

#### `sync_downlink_log`

What the cloud told us and what we did about it. When a customer says "I paid   but I am still not connected", this table plus subscription_events in the cloud   pinpoints which link broke: payment recorded but not synced, synced but CoA   failed, or CoA sent and the router ignored it. Without it that conversation is   guesswork.

| Column | Type | Null | Default / Generated | Keys & constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `bigserial` | no |  | **PK** |
| `source` | `text` | no |  | CHECK |
| `entity` | `text` | no |  |  |
| `entity_id` | `uuid` | yes |  |  |
| `action` | `text` | no |  | CHECK |
| `rows_affected` | `integer` | no | 0 |  |
| `applied_ms` | `integer` | yes |  |  |
| `error` | `text` | yes |  |  |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |

_Indexes:_
- `sync_downlink_log_brin` — BRIN `created_at`

#### `edge_devices`

Local mirror of the cloud user_devices table, queried by an unlang policy at   Access-Request time:     if ("%{sql:SELECT count(*) FROM edge_devices \          WHERE username='%{User-Name}' \            AND mac_address=UPPER('%{Calling-Station-Id}') \            AND status='allowed'}" == "0") {         update control { Auth-Type := Reject }     }   Two independent controls:     * plans.max_registered_devices caps how many rows a username may have;     * users.mac_binding_enabled / plans.mac_binding_required sets is_bound, which       makes the policy hard-reject any unregistered MAC. This is the control that       actually stops one GH¢70 account serving a whole compound.   NEW MACs are inserted as `pending` and pushed to the cloud via sync_outbox   (kind=device_seen) so the customer can approve them from the portal — the   alternative is a support call for every new phone in the household.   MAC normalisation matters: MikroTik sends Calling-Station-Id lower case with   colons, iOS randomises MACs per SSID by default, and Android does the same. The   portal must tell users to disable "private Wi-Fi address" for this network, or   binding will fight them.

| Column | Type | Null | Default / Generated | Keys & constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `bigserial` | no |  | **PK** |
| `username` | `varchar(64)` | no |  |  |
| `mac_address` | `varchar(17)` | no |  |  |
| `status` | `text` | no | 'pending' | CHECK |
| `is_bound` | `boolean` | no | false |  |
| `first_seen_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |
| `last_seen_at` | `timestamptz` | yes |  |  |
| `last_nas` | `inet` | yes |  |  |
| `cloud_id` | `uuid` | yes |  |  |
| `updated_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |

_Table-level:_ UNIQUE (`username`, `mac_address`)

_Indexes:_
- `edge_devices_mac_idx` — `mac_address`

#### `activation_tokens`

One-time tokens for the ACTIVATION HANDSHAKE (docs/01-architecture.md §1.7).   The problem: the HTTPS portal cannot POST credentials to the router's HTTP   /login endpoint — browsers block a form submission from an https: page to an   http: URL as mixed content. Serving the portal over plain HTTP to dodge that   would put a payment flow on an unencrypted page.   The solution: the portal does a TOP-LEVEL redirect (allowed) to a tiny   router-hosted HTTP page carrying only a token. That page exchanges the token for   credentials at the edge node over the LAN, then submits a SAME-ORIGIN POST to   /login. Credentials never appear in a URL, never cross the satellite link, and   exist for 60 seconds. This is what makes "instant activation, no manual step"   actually work on a phone.   A purge job deletes expired rows every few minutes; the table never grows.

| Column | Type | Null | Default / Generated | Keys & constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `token` | `text` | no |  | **PK** |
| `username` | `text` | no |  |  |
| `password` | `text` | no |  |  |
| `mac_address` | `varchar(17)` | no |  |  |
| `nas_ip` | `inet` | yes |  |  |
| `link_orig` | `text` | yes |  |  |
| `order_id` | `uuid` | yes |  |  |
| `expires_at` | `timestamptz` | no |  |  |
| `consumed_at` | `timestamptz` | yes |  |  |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |

_Indexes:_
- `activation_tokens_expiry_idx` — `expires_at`

#### `edge_config`

Runtime knobs FreeRADIUS and syncd need WITHOUT a cloud round trip: default   session/idle timeout, FUP evaluation interval, CoA retry policy, the walled-garden   revision, and `degraded_mode_auth` — whether to keep authenticating from cache when   the cloud is unreachable. That one defaults to TRUE deliberately: locking paying   customers out during a Starlink obstruction event is a worse outcome than a small   risk of a stale entitlement, and `radius.degraded_mode_max_age_hours` (48) bounds   that risk so a long outage cannot keep a long-expired account online forever.

| Column | Type | Null | Default / Generated | Keys & constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | `text` | no |  | **PK** |
| `value` | `jsonb` | no |  |  |
| `revision` | `integer` | no | 0 |  |
| `updated_at` | `timestamptz` | no | now() |  |
